Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

📡 Chinese envoy: Beijing adopts consistent and stable policy toward Tehran

📌 Tehran, IRNA — China’s ambassador to Tehran has stressed that Beijing’s policy toward Iran remains consistent and stable, reiterating China’s commitment to developing all-out ties.

Addressing the international conference titled Half a Century of Iran–China Diplomatic Relations, Cong Peiwu stressed the continuity and stability of Beijing’s policy toward Tehran.
​
China was prepared to advance bilateral relations along a stable and sustainable path by strengthening communication with Iran, he added.
​
Over the past 55 years, bilateral relations have withstood the challenges arising from evolving international dynamics and fluctuations in the global political landscape, maintaining a stable and constructive trajectory of development, he stated.
​
China and Iran have firmly supported each other on issues concerning their respective fundamental interests and major concerns, he stressed.
​
They have also maintained active exchanges and cooperation in the economic, commercial, cultural, and humanitarian fields, Peiwu said.
​
China and Iran are both developing countries and members of the Global South. Both are also members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the BRICS, and both work to advance an international order that is fairer and more rational, the diplomat reiterated.
​
Commenting on China’s position on peace, security, and the independence of the Middle East, he said this year, amid continued instability and tensions in the Middle East, President Xi Jinping has put forward a series of initiatives and proposals aimed at establishing peace and stability in the region.
​
These initiatives provide a systematic approach to advancing political solutions to Middle Eastern issues and achieving lasting peace and stability in the region, he added.
​
The Middle East belongs to the people of the Middle East, he said, stressing that authority and the initiative in regional security affairs should rest with the regional countries and be exercised independently by them.
​
The first international conference on Half a Century of Iran–China Diplomatic Relations was held at the University of Tehran.
​
The event was organized by the university’s Center for Graduate International Studies and featured a video address by Iran’s ambassador to China, as well as presentations by professors and experts specializing in China and East Asia.

PPI shows how prices are changing for businesses themselves. When production, energy, transportation, and other costs go up, some of those increases are usually passed on to consumers over time. On top of that, the previous day’s consumer inflation report also came in hotter than expected. In other words, there have now been two consecutive signals that the U.S. inflation problem isn’t going away.

This is bad news for markets for a very simple reason. The higher inflation is, the less room the Fed has to cut rates, and the more likely interest rates are to stay elevated for longer. High rates are particularly painful for tech companies, crypto, and other assets that depend more heavily on cheap money and liquidity.

Part of the recent spike is indeed tied to energy prices, which jumped 10.8% in a single month. So it’s too early to call this a new inflation crisis based on one data point. But the problem is that price increases are showing up in other areas too, which means it’s not possible to blame everything on oil alone.

For Bitcoin over the long term, a single report doesn’t fundamentally change anything. But over the next few weeks, data like this increases the likelihood of pressure across the broader crypto market. The same goes for stocks, especially tech stocks.

That’s why it’s best not to rush into buying every dip right now. It makes more sense to keep some capital in cash and be prepared to buy quality assets at lower prices if the pressure continues. The long-term thesis remains unchanged, but in the short term, the market has one more reason to move lower.

Panama has introduced a 12-month Working Holiday visa for young foreigners

Panama has created a new visa in the non-resident category that allows young foreigners to stay in the country for up to 12 months and work temporarily under the "Vacaciones y Trabajo" program (Working Holiday). The corresponding Executive Decree No. 21 of October 13, 2026, was published in the Official Gazette on October 14 and came into effect on the same day.

The visa is only available to citizens of countries with which Panama has bilateral agreements under this program. Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years old at the time of application. The duration of stay is up to 12 months without the possibility of extension. After the program ends, the foreigner must leave the country.

Separate permission from the Ministry of Labor and Labor Development (Mitradel) is required to engage in paid work. The decree explicitly prohibits engaging in permanent work activities and applying for residency during the visa's validity period. Changing immigration categories is also not allowed.

Documents required include a notarized copy of the passport, three photographs, an apostilled birth certificate and a police clearance certificate from the country of origin, a certificate from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirming participation in the program, medical insurance for the entire stay, and proof of sufficient funds to sustain oneself in Panama.

The new visa differs from the Remote Workers visa introduced in 2021, which is meant for those who solely earn income from abroad and do not work in the Panamanian labor market.
